content:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday continued defending Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and his administration over last week’s nationwide flight shutdown — only to reveal that he had personally halted necessary improvements to the system.

Trump openly admitted as much during a Fox News interview from China, brazenly arguing that the $12.5 billion approved by a Republican-led Congress last year, specifically to modernize the Federal Aviation Administration’s air traffic system, wasn’t enough to start.

“And, you know, we were given $12 billion, but I said, ‘Don’t spend it until we can do the whole thing, the whole system,’” Trump said Wednesday. “You don’t want to do piecemeal, that’s what they did before. I build, I build very well, I made a lot of money building things.”

He added, “I know how to do this stuff. And I said, ‘Don’t.’ I think Sean’s doing fantastic, Sean Duffy. I think the whole group is doing great. But I said, ‘Don’t waste the money by building little this and that’ … We want to give out one big [expenditure], like the ‘big, beautiful’ deal.”

Trump said he wants to give “somebody” one contract to “coordinate everything,” stating the current FAA system uses copper and “glass wiring.” The MAGA leader previously decried this on Monday and blamed former President Joe Biden’s administration for the shutdown.

“A first-year engineering student would know that you don’t hook up — they spent billions of dollars, the previous administration, and then they tried to hook it up and it didn’t work,” Trump said Wednesday. “Not only didn’t it work, it set it back.”

It’s important to note that domestic and international air travel concerning the U.S. was running smoothly until last week’s unnerving ground stop, which Trump has also recently blamed on former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg — who swiftly fired back with facts.

Friday’s shutdown lasted more than four hours and affected 1.5 million passengers on some 11,000 flights. Duffy blamed it on old FAA equipment, while Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said an attempt to transition to a “new technology” could be to blame.

Mullin also said there was “zero evidence” at the time that it was caused by cyberattacks. He told Fox News on Monday that the ground stop and recent tech outages may have been spurred by artificial intelligence, however, and that its “self-fixing” nature “overran” the systems.

Duffy had announced days earlier that the FAA was expanding its AI-based platform SMART (or Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories), but confidently claimed Friday that “there’s no possible way” this contributed to the shutdown.

“So, we want it fixed, and we want it fixed right,” Trump said Wednesday about the FAA. “And we don’t want to spend drips and drabs, we want to get one big — whether it’s a Raytheon or an IBM or, you know, there are numerous companies that are fantastic in this.”

He continued, “But you can’t do it in drips and drabs.”

Just why the seemingly pressing issue can’t be addressed incrementally remains unclear. Trump on Wednesday provided an apparent timeline for a permanent fix, seemingly confirming that the project won’t be finished for “a couple of years.”

Critics were quick to mock him, as Trump had praised Duffy’s “fantastic” job performance following the longest FAA ground stop since 9/11 — and tried promising his dwindling bastion of supporters that America will soon have “the best system anywhere in the world.”
